text:
Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: History of Jamaica Plain, Boston
Tour-Category: book

Stop 1: Jamaica Pond

Address: Jamaica Pond, Boston, MA 02130

Coordinates: 42.3083, -71.1151

Type/Specialty: Scenic Park

Specific Examples: Beautiful pond views, walking paths, and diverse bird species.

Orientation: You are about to embark on a walking journey through the History of Jamaica Plain, Boston. Your first stop is Jamaica Pond. From the Forest Hills T Station, walk northeast on Washington St toward Jamaica Pond. Turn left onto Jamaica Pond Path. After a short walk, you'll arrive at Jamaica Pond, where you can enjoy the tranquil waters and surrounding nature. Stand on the northern shore of Jamaica Pond, where the wind stirs the water into shifting patterns of light and a chorus of oarlocks and distant voices carries across the open surface.

Jamaica Pond’s mirror stillness belies the restless activity that has shaped the land around it. In the 1650s, the Curtis family — one of Jamaica Plain’s oldest lineages — established themselves here, purchasing land from the Greenough estate in 1868. Their presence signaled the transformation from wild edge to cultivated ground, a transition echoing the ambitions of the era. By 1800, this area remained a quiet agricultural and residential district, a few miles west of Boston’s pulse, its farms and estates defining the landscape. The story of a Massachusetts Bay Governor from 1760 to 1769 is woven into the fabric of this place. A prominent figure of the time maintained a summer residence on Pond Street, where a sixty-acre estate overlooked these waters. The pond’s proximity to Boston provided respite while keeping its residents within reach of the city’s affairs, a balance that mirrored the neighborhood’s future: both urban refuge and site of power. In the decades that followed, Jamaica Plain would become one of the first streetcar suburbs in America, its fortunes tied to the expanding reach of Boston itself. The surface of Jamaica Pond shimmers with today’s sunlight, but beneath it lie the memory of those who came before — Curtis and Greenough, Bernard and the many who followed — each leaving their marks in land, in law, and in the shifting boundaries of the city.

Directions: Turn left onto South Street, and keep an eye out for the charming Loring-Greenough House on your right, nestled among the trees. It is roughly 550 meters away.

Stop 2: Loring-Greenough House

Address:

Coordinates: 42.3132, -71.1145

Type/Specialty: Historic House Museum

Specific Examples: Historic architecture, period furnishings, and beautiful gardens.

Orientation:

Here’s the secret they almost never say aloud over coffee: in 1760, Commodore Joshua Loring built this house as a statement of Loyalist ambition, every board and pane chosen to declare his place in the colonial order. But that elegant façade, all symmetry and polished wood, hides stories of upheaval and uneasy alliances. The Lorings’ world—like the very boundaries of Jamaica Plain, which today claims 4.4 square miles within Boston—was never as settled as it looked. Now for the whisper behind the wallpaper: this house is a site of enslavement. At least three people—London, Othello, and Phillis—were owned by the Loring family. Their names survive in the record, but the rest is silence: what it meant to pass through these rooms not as a guest but as property, to work beneath the same ceilings that later echoed with talk of liberty and revolution. There’s another tale, and it’s as tangled as the honeysuckle along the porch. After the Lorings, the Greenough family held the house from 1783 until 1924. The neighborhood, which seceded from Roxbury in 1851 and joined Boston in 1874, changed around the Greenoughs, but the house remained, its walls absorbing the city’s shifting allegiances. What you hear now—the crunch of gravel, the distant call of a blue jay, the faint rumble from Centre Street—links you to every character who moved through this house. Their fortunes rose and fell with the tides of history, their choices shaping the Jamaica Plain you walk through today. The Loring-Greenough House is less a monument than a palimpsest: its layers of loss, adaptation, and survival are written in every floorboard under your feet.

Directions: From the Loring-Greenough House, stroll down South Street, taking in the charming historic homes along the way. As you continue, keep an eye out for the entrance to Forest Hills Cemetery on your right, marked by its beautiful wrought-iron gate. Enjoy the peaceful atmosphere as you make your way to this serene final resting place. It is roughly 1.2 km (about a 14-minute walk) away.

Stop 3: Forest Hills Cemetery

Address: 95 Forest Hills Ave, Jamaica Plain, MA 02130

Coordinates: 42.3049, -71.1061

Type/Specialty: Cemetery and Arboretum

Specific Examples: Stunning monuments, serene walking paths, and diverse tree species.

Orientation: As you stand just inside the gates of Forest Hills Cemetery, listen for the hush that settles beneath the wide branches and the shifting gravel underfoot. Here, in the garden cemetery’s winding lanes and scattered sunlight, the boundaries between past and present feel porous—names and dates carved in stone amid the green.

Forest Hills Cemetery has belonged to Jamaica Plain since 1848, created to replace older graveyards and offer a new kind of space for remembrance. This ground has witnessed the neighborhood transform—from the early days when families like William Heath’s settled south of Parker Hill in the 1600s, to the Jamaica Plain of today, a 4.4-square-mile neighborhood within Boston, with more than 41,000 residents as counted in 2020. The same community whose rhythms you glimpsed at the Loring-Greenough House now comes here in procession and in pause.

In October 1893, Lucy Stone died—her name familiar to anyone who has read about abolition and women’s rights. What happened next was unusual for its day: Stone’s body was kept in cold storage for over two months, her family pausing the rituals of burial. On December 30, 1893, she was cremated, a choice that marked both a break from tradition and a statement about how legacies might endure or be transformed.

A short walk away, the tale of Louise Mieusset and her son, Louis Ernest Mieusset, speaks of the hardships that shadow even the quietest graves. Louis Ernest died in 1886, reportedly from scarlet fever and acute nephritis. Decades later, in 1936, his mother Louise died destitute and was first buried in an unmarked pauper’s grave. The story goes that Mayor James Michael Curley intervened, arranging for Louise to be buried beside her son—a gesture that joined their names in this ground after hardship had kept them apart.

The stones here do not simply record endings. They hold the traces of choices and interventions—rituals interrupted, losses answered, and the quiet work of a community that, even in mourning, makes itself visible.

Directions: Start by leaving Forest Hills Cemetery and head down South Street. As you stroll, keep an eye out for the beautiful Victorian homes lining the street. When you reach the intersection with Washington Street, continue straight, and soon you’ll see the Samuel Adams Brewery on your right, nestled behind some trees. Enjoy the walk! It is roughly 400 meters away.

Stop 4: Samuel Adams Brewery

Address:

Coordinates: 42.3081, -71.1040

Type/Specialty: Brewery

Specific Examples: Brewery tours, tasting room, and beer garden.

Orientation: Stand at the mouth of Germania Street, where the red-brick mass of the Samuel Adams Brewery rises against the sky. The cooling breeze carries a faint scent of hops and malt, drifting from the loading bay. Overhead, the angular outline of old industrial windows hints at a world within, where barrels and copper tanks have outlasted generations.

Where you now see the Samuel Adams name, this ground once rang with the machinery of the Haffenreffer brewery, built in the nineteenth century by Rudolf Haffenreffer. The present-day brewery takes its label from Samuel Adams, the Founding Father who inherited his father’s malt-house on Boston’s King Street, now State Street. Before his name was attached to revolution, Adams was a brewer or maltster; this connection was chosen by Jim Koch, who founded the Boston Beer Company in Cambridge in 1984. Five generations of Koch men had brewed before him, but it was Jim who revived the family tradition, brewing the first test batches of what would become Samuel Adams Boston Lager in his home kitchen. Those early boil-overs sent wallpaper peeling from his kitchen walls, the mess a kind of baptism by malt and steam.

The physical legacy of the past lingers here — echoes of the old brewery, the ghosts of workers and barrels, a neighborhood shaped by industrial labor. The beer that fills these vats now is not just product, but a continuation of a line: Samuel Adams, the man; Jim Koch, the brewer; and the generations in between, each leaving their mark. In this way, the Samuel Adams Brewery stands as living proof of Jamaica Plain’s ability to reforge itself. Where Forest Hills Cemetery memorializes those who have passed, the brewery distills the spirit of those who persist — flavor and memory, layered in each glass. The air tastes of history and change, and with each batch, something old becomes new again.

Together, these stops reveal the layered history of Jamaica Plain, where the echoes of past lives and choices shape the present. Understanding this tapestry of transformation invites us to reflect on how our own actions contribute to the ongoing story of the community. That's 4 stops in all.
